old: The first law states that energy can be neither created nor destroyed. Its mathematical form is $\Delta U = q + w$, using the convention that q and w are positive when heat or work enters the system. Pressure-volume work is $w = -p_{ext}\Delta V$. Expansion against zero external pressure (free expansion) gives w = 0. For reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, $w = -2.303nRT\log\frac{V_2}{V_1}$, and because $\Delta U = 0$, it follows that $q = -w$. For an adiabatic process, $\Delta U = w$. Internal energy is the heat exchanged at constant volume ($\Delta U = q_V$). Enthalpy is defined as H = U + pV, and its change equals the heat exchanged at constant pressure ($\Delta H = q_p$). For gaseous reactions, $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$. Here $\Delta n_g$ is the moles of gaseous products minus the moles of gaseous reactants.

Its mathematical form is $\Delta U = q + w$, using the convention that q and w are positive when heat or work enters the system. Pressure-volume work is $w = -p_{ext}\Delta V$. Expansion against zero external pressure (free expansion) gives w = 0. The change in internal energy equals the heat exchanged at constant volume ($\Delta U = q_V$). Enthalpy is defined as H = U + pV, and its change equals the heat exchanged at constant pressure ($\Delta H = q_p$). For gaseous reactions, $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$. Here $\Delta n_g$ is the moles of gaseous products minus the moles of gaseous reactants.
